clue.text: Brook's sequel to Psycho?

definitions.note: possessive: the noise a brook makes
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the murmuring sound of a running stream

definitions.note: the word that follows 'psycho' in a compound
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the second half of the compound for pseudo-scientific therapy jargon

explanation.surface: Sounds like a film critic asking what a director called Brook made after Hitchcock's Psycho.
explanation.walkthrough: Brook looks like a person's name (Peter Brook, the director), but it is a stream; psychobabble is the jargon of pop psychology.
explanation.definitionFit: A stream murmurs and gurgles over stones, and pop-psychology jargon is called psychobabble, so the word fits both senses.

clue.text: Primate's presidential project?

parts.note: George W. Bush became US President in 2001
a pet project is someone's 'baby'

explanation.surface: A president's favourite scheme, attributed to a primate.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is'. Read the wordplay as 'Bush's baby', the President's pet scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: The galago, a small nocturnal African primate with huge eyes, is commonly called by this name.

clue.text: American right (it stresses) — no long sleeves here, say?
Probe some unlikely consequence

indicators.note: a consequence is what results, here the letters reshaped by the unlikely order
only some of the following word is used, the tail being dropped

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An investigation turns up a surprising result.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the first five letters of 'unlikely', UNLIK, and rearrange them. 'Unlikely' also hints at the jumble. Lunik was the Soviet series of Moon probes of 1959.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunik was the Western name for the Soviet Luna spacecraft sent to the Moon, an unmanned space probe.

clue.text: Ordinary sort of lamp

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a tall lamp on a pole standing on the floor

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase, an ordinary lamp, but splits into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means normal or regular, and a tall floor-standing lamp is called by this name in British English.

clue.text: One standing a round — around students out of town on Cromarty Firth — making no progress

indicators.note: the round-buyer goes around, enclosing the town that follows

parts.note: someone who stands a round of drinks treats the company

indicators.note: the students are taken out of the town's name

parts.note: Dingwall is a Scottish town at the head of the Cromarty Firth
L for learner, twice

explanation.surface: A pub round bought among students in a Highland town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing a round' means buying drinks for others; L is the learner plate on British cars, so students are L's.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone keeping afloat in one spot without swimming anywhere stays put, the idiom for marking time and failing to advance.

clue.text: Ass anaesthetises selective slaughter, say

indicators.note: 'say' signals that the last part is to be taken by its sound, then spelt differently

parts.note: an anaesthetic numbs the patient
a cull is the selective killing of animals

explanation.surface: A donkey drugged before a cull of the herd.
explanation.walkthrough: Ass is the fool, not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupid person is called an ass, and a thickhead or blockhead is the same kind of dimwit.

clue.text: When he turns up, it's a model he needs

definitions.text: When he turns up, it's a model he needs

parts.words: When he turns up, it's a model he needs
parts.note: surface: someone arriving who needs an example to follow
setter's reading: a painter in the studio needs a sitter to pose

explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' suggests a pattern to copy; it is the person who poses for a painter or sculptor.
explanation.definitionFit: Painters and sculptors work from a sitter posing in the studio, so such a creator needs a model when arriving.

clue.text: Quite good translation of 100

parts.note: surface padding that tells you to put the next words into French
French for 'of'
French for a hundred

explanation.surface: Praise for a rendering of a number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Translation' tells you to put 'of 100' into French: de cent.
explanation.definitionFit: Something satisfactory or acceptable without being excellent is described as reasonably good, adequate.

clue.text: Rustic beau with son on cart

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son
a wain is an old word for a farm wagon

explanation.surface: A country suitor riding with his boy on a farm cart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' means placed before the cart in this across answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In pastoral poetry a young country lover or suitor courting a shepherdess is called by this old word.

clue.text: Can impute suffering to being blown up

indicators.note: something suffering is in a bad way, so the letters are knocked out of shape

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone can blame suffering on being blown up by a bomb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blown up' suggests an explosion; here it means inflated with air.
explanation.definitionFit: Tyres and similar things filled with compressed air are described by this adjective, meaning inflated by air.

clue.text: Box for money? Navy pilot I see will arrange it

indicators.note: arranging the preceding words means setting their letters in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A naval aviator promises to sort out a boxing match for cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' is British slang for the television set.
explanation.definitionFit: The box is the TV, and subscription channels charge the viewer money, hence telly you pay for.

clue.text: Servant in country going to America with name of flower dear to 17

indicators.note: one thing set in another means it goes inside it

parts.note: Beds is the short name for Bedfordshire, an English county
a lackey is a footman or menial servant
the usual abbreviation
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A rural servant emigrates to the US, with a flower's name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country' stretches to the county: Bedfordshire, an English county, is written Beds. John Gay's ballad pairs Sweet William with Black-eyed Susan.
explanation.definitionFit: This yellow daisy-like rudbeckia is named after the heroine of Gay's ballad, the sweetheart of the sailor William at 17.

clue.text: See 11
Buy factory — any hesitation? Reportedly, we've just begun another one

definitions.note: a clause describing the answer rather than a noun

indicators.note: 'reportedly' tells you the words are heard, so the spelling follows the sound

parts.note: the verb, spelt as the Latin-derived prefix for two
a mill is a factory
the word sounds roughly like 'enny'
the sound made when hesitating

explanation.surface: A takeover bid for a factory, with a pause before the deal.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle appeared in 2001, just after the year 2000 marked two thousand years of the Christian era.
explanation.definitionFit: A period of two thousand years, or its anniversary; the year 2000 had just started a new such period when this appeared.

clue.text: Some flowers to beautify ratings' quarters?

indicators.note: only some of the next word is wanted, so its outer letters are dropped

parts.note: taken as written
to deck is to adorn or decorate

explanation.surface: Flowers are used to brighten the crew's cabins.
explanation.walkthrough: Ratings are ordinary sailors, not officers, in the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: On a warship the ordinary seamen, rather than the officers, live below on the lowest level, so the term names them and their quarters.

clue.text: The scandal of dreamer Walter? They say not to take it so seriously

definitions.text: not to take it so seriously
definitions.note: loosely: to make it less serious

indicators.note: what 'they say' is heard rather than read, so take the sound of the phrase

parts.note: Walter Mitty is Thurber's daydreamer, and scandals take the suffix -gate after Watergate

explanation.surface: Gossip about a fantasist's disgrace, with advice to calm down.
explanation.walkthrough: Walter Mitty is the daydreaming hero of James Thurber's story; any scandal gets '-gate' added after Watergate.
explanation.definitionFit: To lessen the severity or gravity of something, making an offence count for less, is to soften it.

clue.text: Irish 6, love-crazy one taken in by barbarian

definitions.note: 6 is NUMBSKULL, so an Irish fool

indicators.note: one thing taken in by another is held inside it

parts.note: zero, as in a tennis score
a direct synonym
the Huns were barbarian invaders
a means one

explanation.surface: An Irish fool, mad with love, is captured by a savage.
explanation.walkthrough: A goes inside HUN. The word comes from Irish amadán, a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hiberno-English this word, from Gaelic amadán, means a fool or idiot, the Irish equivalent of a dimwit.

clue.text: Little fabric in Asian country for flower dear to 11 12

indicators.note: one thing set in another means it goes inside it

parts.note: Siam is the old name for Thailand
Scottish for small
a twill is a woven cloth with diagonal ribs

explanation.surface: A scrap of cloth found in an Asian land.
explanation.walkthrough: Wee is Scots for small. In John Gay's ballad, William is the sailor loved by Black-eyed Susan.
explanation.definitionFit: This garden pink, Dianthus barbatus, shares its name with the sailor sweetheart of Susan in Gay's ballad.

clue.text: Near time to be outed from it?

parts.note: close means near
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Is the time approaching to come out?
explanation.walkthrough: To be outed is to be forced out of the closet, that is, to have one's homosexuality revealed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hiding their sexuality is said to be in the cupboard of this name, and being outed drags them from it.

clue.text: Aids for drinkers 21
Retaliation beginning from the right in due course

indicators.note: reading from the right means right to left, backwards
only the beginning of the word is kept, its tail dropped

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Revenge, begun by the political right, will come in time.
explanation.walkthrough: Keep the first five letters, RETAL, and read them backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Something happening afterwards, at a subsequent time, happens eventually or in due course.

clue.text: Dylan's answer likely?

parts.note: surface: what a poet named Dylan would probably reply
setter's reading: Bob Dylan's song says the answer is blowing somewhere

explanation.walkthrough: Bob Dylan sang 'The answer, my friend, is blowin' ...'; 'likely' fits because something in the offing is about to happen.
explanation.definitionFit: Something likely or impending is said to be in the offing, using an idiom that also completes Dylan's famous refrain.

clue.text: John with candle 21

parts.note: surface: some man called John holding a candle
setter's reading: the singer whose hit was a candle with the 21 phrase

explanation.walkthrough: 21 is IN THE WIND, so the song is 'Candle in the Wind', sung by Elton John.
explanation.definitionFit: The singer-songwriter whose surname is John recorded the famous ballad, so his first name is the answer.

clue.text: More pompous part of 7's workshop

indicators.note: only part of the cross-referenced word is used, its front cut away

parts.note: 7 down's answer
an atelier is a painter's studio

explanation.surface: A grand claim made in the corner of a painter's studio.
explanation.walkthrough: Keep only the tail of the 7 answer and add the French-derived word for a studio.
explanation.definitionFit: Stately means grand and dignified, and its comparative suits someone behaving with more pomp and self-importance.

clue.text: Nanki-poo's sequel to spring flowers

parts.note: surface: blooms that come after spring flowers
setter's reading: the refrain following a line in The Mikado

explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado, 'The flowers that bloom in the spring' is followed by this nonsense refrain; Nanki-Poo is one of the singers.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's line about blossoms of the season ends with this cheerful nonsense refrain, which follows it every time.

clue.text: Facial hair on landscape gardener in central Asia

parts.note: British slang for a moustache
William Kent, the 18th-century landscape garden designer

explanation.surface: A moustached garden designer at work in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent also looks like the English county, but here it is William Kent of Stowe and Rousham gardens.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital of Uzbekistan is a city located in the heart of the region between the Caspian and China.

clue.text: Exercise in translation: our German doesn't end in French

indicators.note: a word that does not end has lost its final letter

parts.note: German for 'our'
French for 'in'

explanation.surface: A language lesson in which German and French get muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: An unseen is a passage set for translation without preparation, common in British school exams.
explanation.definitionFit: In language exams a passage given to translate at sight, not studied beforehand, is called by this noun.
